transcript.speaker: KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)
transcript.text:
ATTEMPT. This distinction between particularity and grounding has been drawn by Niko Kolodny in "Which Relationships Justify Partiality?" (2003) and developed in his later work. Kolodny explicitly argues that we can have reasons to benefit particular persons that are both derivative (grounded in more general values like shared history or intimacy) and yet irreducibly particular (not substitutable). He calls these "relationship-dependent" reasons and contrasts them with both impersonal consequentialist reasons and non-derivative personal reasons. The weak point in the candidate thesis is the claim that this separates "the anti-fungibility intuition from the grounding question" as if this were a novel observation—Kolodny's entire framework rests on showing that particularity (what he calls the "specially-directed" character of reasons) can be explained by features of the relationship without requiring final value. Troy Jollimore's work on love also explores how derivative accounts can preserve particularity through historical and narrative features. The candidate presents as a fresh distinction what is actually a well-established position in the literature on special obligations.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis claims to identify a conflation that "both sides" make, but one major side (the derivative view as articulated by Kolodny) explicitly rejects this conflation. The thesis survives only if reformulated as a criticism of *some* participants, not the debate's structure itself.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
BEST DEFENCE

The objection misreads the dialectical target. Kolodny's framework does not rescue the candidate thesis—it *exemplifies* it. The claim is not "no one has noticed these are separate" but "the debate wrongly treats them as packaged together." Kolodny's contribution is precisely to show they come apart, which means he's on the *same side* as this thesis, not a counterexample to it.

Look at what the objection concedes: Kolodny argues particularity can be derivative. That's exactly the thesis's point. The "conflation" being diagnosed is the assumption that if you want particularity, you must buy non-derivativeness (the final value view), or if you accept derivativeness, you must surrender particularity to impersonal welfare (crude consequentialism). Kolodny breaks this package deal. So does this thesis.

The objection says "the candidate presents as a fresh distinction what is actually a well-established position." But the candidate never claims novelty. It claims the distinction is *orthogonal* and that *both sides conflate* the dimensions. If Kolodny has established the position, that supports rather than undermines the thesis—it shows the distinction can be drawn and that doing so reframes the debate. The thesis is a diagnostic move about how the debate has been structured, not a claim to have invented the resources for restructuring it.

The real question is whether the "both sides" framing holds. Does the final value camp also conflate these? Yes: they typically argue "if friendship matters as *Jane's* good specifically, this can't be derivative from general concern for persons, so it must have final value." That's precisely treating particularity and non-derivativeness as a package. The thesis identifies this as the shared mistake.

VERDICT

The defence fails, but not for the reason the objection gives.

The problem is that the objection is right about the dialectical situation even though wrong about what it shows. If Kolodny's work explicitly separates particularity from non-derivativeness, then the thesis cannot claim "both sides conflate" these dimensions—at least one major position has already drawn the distinction. 

The thesis survives only as: "One side of the debate (the final value view) wrongly assumes particularity requires non-derivativeness, while the other side (derivative views like Kolodny's) has already separated them." But this transforms the thesis from a structural diagnosis of the whole debate into a partisan claim that one side has the better framework. That's not the same move—and it's much weaker, because it's no longer revealing a hidden assumption shared across positions but simply taking a side in an existing dispute.

The thesis is dead as stated. It diagnoses a conflation that isn't actually shared.

transcript.speaker: KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)
transcript.text:
ATTEMPT. If this distinction successfully shows that both sides conflate orthogonal questions, the same argumentative structure would apply to virtually every philosophical debate involving both metaphysical grounding and phenomenological features. Consider: "Both sides in the free will debate conflate whether actions matter morally and whether they matter *as that particular agent's* actions rather than as instances of generic behavior." Or: "Both sides in aesthetics conflate whether beauty matters intrinsically and whether it matters *as that particular object's* beauty rather than as an instance of generic aesthetic value." The weak point is the claim that identifying two conceptually separable dimensions (grounding vs. particularity) constitutes finding a *conflation* in the debate. This argumentative move proves too much because any debate involving both "what grounds X" and "what features X has" could be reframed as both sides "conflating" these questions. If successful, this would mean nearly every normative debate that discusses both metaphysical structure and phenomenological character involves a fundamental conflation—making the concept of conflation too cheap. The thesis would license treating any failure to explicitly separate every conceptually distinguishable dimension as a "conflation," turning a substantive diagnostic claim into a mere observation that philosophers discuss multiple related issues simultaneously.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This has some force but limited damage. The thesis could respond that not every case of discussing related dimensions constitutes conflation—only cases where treating them as packaged leads to genuine confusion or false dichotomies. The friendship debate may genuinely suffer from this packaging in a way that matters dialectically, unlike the generic cases.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
# BEST DEFENCE

The objection mistakes a logical possibility (that any debate *could* be reframed this way) for evidence that this reframing is equally trivial in all cases. But conflation is not just "discussing related issues simultaneously" — it's treating conceptually distinct questions as if they have a forced answer-pattern that generates false dilemmas.

The test is dialectical damage. Does the alleged conflation actually trap participants in a bad choice? In friendship, yes: the literature repeatedly presents the choice as "either friendship has final value (and thus captures particularity) or it's derivative (and thus reduces to impersonal welfare-promotion)." This packages particularity with non-derivativeness, making it seem like you must choose between robust particularity and metaphysical economy. Kolodny's work (as the previous objection noted) explicitly breaks this package — which shows the conflation was real enough to need breaking.

The free will case doesn't work the same way. No one thinks you must choose between "actions matter morally OR they matter as that agent's actions." These aren't presented as competing positions that package moral significance with particularity. The aesthetic case is closer but still different: the debate about whether beauty is intrinsic vs. response-dependent doesn't typically present "it matters as *this object's* beauty" as something you must sacrifice if you take the response-dependent view.

The objection's cases are conceptual distinctions that *could* be confused, not distinctions that *are generating false dichotomies in the actual debate*. The thesis identifies a conflation that has dialectical consequences — it structures how positions are presented and what seems like a forced choice. That's not "too cheap" — it's identifying a real structural feature of how this particular debate has developed.

The "proves too much" worry only works if the thesis claims that *any* failure to separate dimensions is a conflation. But the thesis is narrower: it claims *this debate* treats these dimensions as packaged in a way that creates a false dilemma. Whether other debates do this is a separate empirical question about those debates.

# VERDICT

The defence holds, but barely, and the thesis remains mortally wounded by the previous objection.

The defence successfully shows that not every conceptual distinction generates a dialectically significant conflation — only those that actually trap participants in false choices. The friendship debate does seem to present "final value + particularity" vs. "derivative + impersonal" as the main options, which would make the conflation real.

But this defence cannot save the thesis from its fatal problem: the "both sides conflate" framing is false. As the previous objection established, Kolodny's derivative view explicitly separates these dimensions. So at most, one side (the final value view) conflates them while the other side has already drawn the distinction.

The thesis could survive in weakened form: "The final value view wrongly assumes particularity requires non-derivativeness, missing that derivative accounts like Kolodny's can preserve particularity." But this is no longer a structural diagnosis of a shared assumption — it's just a criticism of one position for ignoring an available alternative.

The "proves too much" objection fails to kill the thesis independently, but the thesis is already dead from the previous wound. You cannot diagnose a conflation as structuring "both sides" of a debate when one side has explicitly rejected that conflation.

transcript.speaker: KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)
transcript.text:
ATTEMPT. Consider the debate over whether aesthetic value is intrinsic or response-dependent. The candidate's argumentative structure claims to identify a conflation by separating two dimensions: whether something matters for its own sake vs. whether it matters as *that particular thing's* feature. Applied to aesthetics: "Both sides conflate whether beauty matters intrinsically and whether it matters *as that particular object's* beauty rather than as an instance of generic aesthetic value." But this is not how the aesthetic debate actually works. Response-dependent theorists don't claim that a painting's beauty matters merely as an instance of generic aesthetic value—they maintain it matters as *this painting's* beauty, grounded in our responses to this particular object's features. Similarly, in debates about promissory obligations, no one thinks that accepting promises as derivative from a practice of promise-keeping means your promise to *Jane specifically* becomes fungible with promises to anyone. The weak point is the thesis's implicit claim that derivative views *typically* or *structurally* lose particularity. But the actual pattern in normative philosophy is that derivative accounts routinely preserve particularity through historical, relational, or contextual features. The friendship debate isn't special—most derivative accounts in ethics maintain that what's grounded in general principles can still matter as *this particular instance*. The thesis misidentifies a general feature of derivative reasoning as a specific conflation in friendship ethics.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — This is a genuine problem that needs answering. The counterexamples show that derivative accounts commonly preserve particularity across multiple domains, which undermines the claim that the friendship debate involves an unusual conflation. However, the thesis could respond that even if derivative views *can* preserve particularity in principle, the friendship debate has historically presented the choice as a forced package deal in a way these other debates haven't.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
# BEST DEFENCE

The objection grants exactly what the thesis needs: that derivative accounts *can* preserve particularity. The question is whether the friendship debate has *recognized* this or instead structured itself around a false dichotomy.

The counterexamples actually support the thesis. In aesthetics, response-dependence theorists explicitly maintain that *this painting's* beauty matters as such, not as generic aesthetic value. In promissory obligation, theorists routinely distinguish the practice-based grounding from the particular-promisee directedness. These debates got it right—they separated the dimensions. The friendship debate, by contrast, has historically presented the choice as: "Either friendship has final value (Velleman, Kolodny's opponents) or it reduces to concern for persons generally (crude consequentialism)."

Look at the actual dialectic. The final value theorists argue: "If Jane's good mattered merely derivatively—grounded in general concern for persons—then Jane would be replaceable by anyone else who could satisfy that general concern. So to capture friendship's particularity, we need final value." This explicitly packages particularity with non-derivativeness. The objection says "derivative accounts routinely preserve particularity," but that's the point—the final value theorists *deny* this is possible, which is why they insist on final value.

The objection claims "the friendship debate isn't special" because other domains show derivative-plus-particular combinations. But this proves the thesis: if other debates successfully separate these dimensions while the friendship debate treats them as packaged, that shows the friendship debate *is* making an error those other debates avoid. The thesis identifies a conflation that doesn't appear in aesthetics or promises precisely because those debates structured themselves better.

The objection's examples are evidence *for* the diagnosis, not against it. They show that separating grounding from particularity is philosophically routine—which makes it more puzzling and significant that the friendship debate has resisted this separation. The thesis explains why: both sides have conflated the dimensions, with final value theorists insisting you need non-derivativeness for particularity, and crude derivative views conceding particularity in pursuit of metaphysical economy.

# VERDICT

The defence fails because it cannot escape the previous fatal objection, and this objection makes the problem worse.

The defence argues that other debates "got it right" by separating the dimensions while the friendship debate hasn't. But this contradicts the thesis's "both sides conflate" framing even more severely. If Kolodny's derivative view explicitly preserves particularity (as the first objection established), then the friendship debate *has* separated these dimensions—at least on one side.

The defence tries to save things by pointing to "final value theorists" who package the dimensions together. But this reduces the thesis to: "One side of the debate makes a mistake that the other side and several other philosophical debates have avoided." That's not a structural diagnosis of a shared conflation—it's just saying one position is wrong.

Worse, the counterexamples reveal that the thesis misidentifies what's distinctive about the friendship debate. If derivative-plus-particular combinations are "philosophically routine" (as the defence concedes), then the real question is not whether the dimensions *can* be separated but whether friendship's particularity has features that *resist* derivative explanation in ways that aesthetic or promissory particularity don't. That's a substantive debate about friendship's nature, not a conflation to be dissolved.

The thesis is dead. It cannot be "both sides conflate" when one side explicitly doesn't, and it cannot be a special insight when the separation is "philosophically routine." At most, it's a criticism of final value theorists for ignoring an available move—but that's a partisan claim in an ongoing dispute, not a diagnostic reframing of the debate's structure.

transcript.speaker: KILLER (TRIVIAL)
transcript.text:
# ATTEMPT

The thesis claims to identify a conflation that structures the friendship debate, but this "discovery" is merely the observation that two conceptually distinct questions are conceptually distinct. The weak point is that separating "matters for its own sake" from "matters as that particular person's good" is a straightforward conceptual exercise, not a substantive insight about friendship ethics.

Any competent philosopher can distinguish metaphysical grounding questions ("what grounds X?") from phenomenological or structural questions ("what features does X have?"). Noting that "whether Jane's good matters derivatively" and "whether it matters as Jane's specifically" are different questions is like noting that "whether water is H2O" and "whether water is wet" are different questions—true, but trivially so once stated.

The thesis presents this conceptual separation as if it reveals a hidden assumption, but it's really just applying a standard philosophical move: take two predicates that could in principle come apart, note they could in principle come apart, declare that people have "conflated" them. This works for any debate: "Both sides conflate whether X is F and whether X is G" is always available whenever F and G are logically independent properties.

The thesis adds no substantive content about friendship, relationships, or value. It's a verbal stipulation—"let's call the grounding question and the particularity question 'orthogonal'"—dressed up as a discovery. The real philosophical work would be showing *why* these dimensions matter for friendship specifically, or *what follows* from separating them. But the thesis merely asserts they're distinct, which is conceptually trivial even if dialectically unnoticed.

# STRENGTH: 2/5

The attack has some force but limited damage. While it's true that the conceptual distinction is straightforward once stated, the thesis could respond that (1) trivial-once-stated doesn't mean dialectically trivial—many important philosophical moves are obvious in retrospect; (2) the claim isn't just that the questions *are* distinct but that treating them as packaged creates false dichotomies with real consequences for theory choice; and (3) even "mere" conceptual clarification can be valuable if it genuinely reframes a debate, which the thesis claims this does.

The thesis survives this attack because identifying a structurally important conflation isn't rendered trivial just by being conceptually simple. However, combined with the previous objections (especially that one side has already drawn this distinction), the thesis remains fatally wounded overall.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
# BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses conceptual simplicity with dialectical triviality. Yes, once stated, the distinction between grounding and particularity is straightforward—but that's true of most important philosophical clarifications. "Validity vs. soundness," "type vs. token," "semantic vs. pragmatic" are all conceptually simple once drawn, yet they do real work in structuring debates.

The test isn't "is this conceptually complex?" but "does drawing it resolve confusions or reframe choices?" The thesis claims it does both. If the debate has genuinely presented "final value + particularity" vs. "derivative + impersonal" as the main options, then showing these dimensions are orthogonal dissolves a false dichotomy. That's not trivial—it's exactly what conceptual distinctions are supposed to do.

The objection says this is "like noting that 'whether water is H2O' and 'whether water is wet' are different questions." But that analogy fails. Those questions don't generate competing theoretical positions or false forced choices. The friendship case does: theorists have explicitly argued "we need final value to capture particularity" and "if it's derivative, it must reduce to impersonal welfare." These aren't just two logically independent properties—they're dimensions that have been *treated as packaged* in ways that structure theory choice.

The objection claims the thesis "adds no substantive content about friendship." But diagnostic moves aren't supposed to add first-order content—they're supposed to clarify the space of positions. If successful, this distinction shows that derivative theorists needn't surrender particularity and final value theorists needn't claim that's the only way to get it. That reframes what the debate is about: not "does friendship have final value?" but "does friendship's particularity require non-derivative grounding or can it be explained by relational/historical features?" That's substantive reframing, not verbal stipulation.

The "always available" worry misses the point. Yes, you can always distinguish logically independent properties, but not every such distinction matters. This one matters if—and only if—the debate has actually conflated these dimensions in ways that generate false choices. The thesis claims it has. Whether that's true is an empirical question about the debate's structure, not something you can dismiss as "trivial" just because the distinction itself is conceptually simple.

# VERDICT

The defence fails, and this objection, combined with the previous ones, confirms the thesis is dead.

The defence tries to argue that conceptual simplicity doesn't entail dialectical triviality, and that's right in principle. But the defence cannot overcome the accumulated damage:

**First**, the thesis cannot claim "both sides conflate" when Kolodny's derivative view explicitly separates these dimensions (first objection). At most, one side makes this mistake.

**Second**, if derivative-plus-particular combinations are "philosophically routine" (third objection), then even the side that allegedly conflates them is simply ignoring an available move, not making a deep structural error.

**Third**, and this objection's real contribution: even if we grant that some theorists have packaged these dimensions, the thesis provides no account of *why* this packaging occurred or *what substantive issue* it obscures. The defence says the distinction "reframes what the debate is about"—from "does friendship have final value?" to "does particularity require non-derivative grounding?" But this isn't a reframing; it's just restating one side's position (Kolodny's) as if it were a neutral clarification.

The thesis fails because it presents as a structural diagnosis what is actually just a description of one position in an ongoing dispute. Kolodny argues: "Particularity doesn't require final value; it can be derivative but still irreducibly particular." The thesis says: "Both sides miss that particularity and grounding are orthogonal." But these aren't the same. The first is a substantive claim about what explains friendship's particularity. The second pretends to be above the fray while actually just endorsing the first.

The conceptual distinction is indeed simple. What's not trivial is the substantive question it was meant to clarify: *Can* derivative accounts genuinely preserve the kind of particularity friendship requires, or does that particularity have features that resist derivative explanation? That's the real debate, and the thesis doesn't resolve it—it just relabels one side's answer as a "conflation" on the other side.

**The thesis is dead.** It cannot be salvaged because its core claim—that both sides share a conflation—is false, and its proposed distinction, while conceptually valid, does no dialectical work beyond restating an existing position.

thesis: Both sides share the false assumption that there is a univocal 'the friend's good' whose value is being disputed, when actually friendship involves commitment to differently-grounded goods: prudential goods of the friend (grounded in their welfare), moral status goods (grounded in personhood), and relationship goods (grounded in the friendship itself), which cannot be assimilated to a single value structure.
sketch: The debate presupposes disputants are arguing about whether THE friend's good has final or derivative value. But 'caring about my friend's good' is not univocal. When I want my friend to avoid pain, I'm responding to a prudential good grounded in sentience. When I respect my friend's autonomy, I'm responding to moral status grounded in personhood. When I want us to have shared experiences, I'm responding to relationship goods grounded in our friendship itself. The first two would matter even if we weren't friends (so they're grounded elsewhere), but the third wouldn't exist without the friendship (and is genuinely friendship-grounded). The debate falsely assumes friendship must give all of these the same value structure. The key premise is that 'the friend's good' picks out a heterogeneous collection rather than a unified object of concern.
target: The shared assumption of both finality and derivative theorists that there is a unified phenomenon whose value structure is being disputed
risk: This might be merely cataloguing distinctions everyone already implicitly recognizes rather than revealing a genuine confusion, or both sides might insist they're only arguing about the genuinely friendship-specific goods

ruling.defence_quality: The defender distinguished between advocating pluralism (a substantive position within the debate) and diagnosing a shared false presupposition (dissolving the debate), arguing the thesis does the latter while existing pluralist literature does the former
ruling.fatal_flaw: The thesis claims to dissolve the debate by diagnosing a shared false presupposition, but it actually makes substantive pluralist claims about value structure (that goods are grounded differently and cannot be unified) which are themselves contested positions within the debate, not neutral diagnoses above it—the thesis participates in the debate while claiming to dissolve it
ruling.promise_reason: Challenges the univocality assumption underlying both positions with a substantive pluralist alternative that could shift how we taxonomize friendship's normative structure.

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims that "the friend's good" is not univocal but rather encompasses multiple types of goods (prudential, moral status, relationship goods). However, this is simply a standard philosophical distinction that both sides of the debate already acknowledge and accommodate. Derivative theorists explicitly recognize that we care about friends' welfare, respect their autonomy, and value shared experiences—they simply argue all these concerns derive from more fundamental moral principles. Finality theorists likewise acknowledge these different aspects of friendship—they argue that friendship itself gives us final reasons to care about all these dimensions of the friend's situation. The thesis presents as a discovery what is actually just a verbal stipulation: relabeling familiar aspects of friendship as "differently-grounded goods" and declaring them "non-assimilable to a single value structure." But both sides already work with these distinctions; they simply disagree about whether friendship provides the ultimate grounding or whether something more fundamental does. The weak point is the claim that disputants falsely assume univocality—in fact, they recognize complexity but offer competing explanations of it. This is taxonomy dressed as insight.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — The attack has some force in that philosophical debates often do accommodate complexity, but the thesis might genuinely identify an unnoticed conflation between different normative structures rather than merely relabeling acknowledged distinctions.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
BEST DEFENCE

The objection misses the structural point. Yes, both sides acknowledge that friendship involves caring about welfare, respecting autonomy, and valuing shared experiences. But they treat these as different ASPECTS of a single normative phenomenon—different ways friendship matters or different things we care about IN friendship. The thesis claims something stronger: these involve fundamentally different VALUE STRUCTURES that cannot be unified.

Consider the difference. Derivative theorists say: "All these concerns (welfare, autonomy, shared experiences) derive from impartial moral principles." Finality theorists say: "All these concerns have their source in the friendship itself." Both answers presuppose the question "What is the value structure of THE friend's good?" makes sense—that there's one answer to give.

But the thesis denies this. The prudential goods aren't grounded in friendship at all—they're grounded in sentience, and would matter even for non-friends. The moral status goods aren't grounded in friendship either—they're grounded in personhood. Only the relationship goods are genuinely friendship-grounded. So when derivative theorists claim friendship's value "derives from" impartial morality, and finality theorists claim it's "finally valuable," they're both trying to give a unified answer to a question that conflates three different normative structures.

The objection says "both sides already work with these distinctions." But working with distinctions between different OBJECTS of concern (welfare vs. autonomy vs. shared experiences) is not the same as recognizing distinctions between different GROUNDS of value. The debate participants think they're disagreeing about whether friendship gives final or derivative reasons to care about the friend's good. The thesis says they're unwittingly asking a malformed question—like asking whether "bank" refers to something natural or artificial when the word is ambiguous between riverbanks and financial institutions.


VERDICT

The defence fails, but not for the reason the objection gives.

The real problem is that the thesis hasn't shown the question is malformed rather than just complex. Even if prudential and moral status goods have grounds outside the friendship, the debate can coherently ask: "Does friendship give us final reasons to care about these goods, or only derivative ones?" 

The finality theorist can say: "Yes, my friend's welfare matters because of sentience, but friendship gives me a special final reason to care about THIS person's welfare." The derivative theorist can say: "Friendship gives you reasons to care, but those reasons derive from impartial duties to respect sentience and personhood, plus perhaps special obligations you've incurred."

The thesis needs to show that these answers are confused or impossible, not merely that the goods have different grounds. But different grounds for goods don't automatically mean different value structures for the reasons friendship gives us regarding those goods. The defence tries to make this leap but doesn't justify it. The debate may be asking one question about a complex phenomenon rather than conflating three questions into a malformed one.

transcript.speaker: KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)
transcript.text:
ATTEMPT. The thesis equivocates on "grounded in" between two readings, and the argument needs both. On one reading, "grounded in" means "has its existence conditions in"—prudential goods exist because of sentience, relationship goods exist because of friendship. On this reading, the claim that these goods have different grounds is plausible and uncontroversial. But on this reading, it's not interesting—the debate can still coherently ask whether friendship gives us final or derivative reasons to care about these differently-sourced goods. On the other reading, "grounded in" means "gets its normative force from"—the reasons to care about these goods derive their authority from different sources. On this reading, the claim would be interesting (it would show the debate question is malformed), but it's not plausible—the thesis provides no argument that because prudential goods exist due to sentience, friendship cannot provide final reasons to care about them. The weak point is the move from "these goods have different existence conditions" to "they cannot be assimilated to a single value structure." This only works if "grounded in" slides between metaphysical and normative readings. The thesis is plausible when "grounds" means existence conditions, interesting when it means normative authority, but the argument cannot establish the interesting claim using only the plausible one.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis needs to show that different grounds of existence entail different value structures, but hasn't bridged that gap without equivocating on what "grounding" means.

transcript.speaker: DEFENDER
transcript.text:
# BEST DEFENCE

The objection claims the thesis equivocates between existence conditions and normative authority. But this gets the dialectical situation backwards. The thesis isn't arguing from "different existence conditions" to "different normative structures." Rather, it's identifying that these goods already have different normative structures, and pointing out that this explains why they have different grounds.

Consider what's actually happening in each case:

**Prudential goods**: The reason pain matters—the source of its normative force—is that pain is bad for sentient beings as such. This is why we have reasons to prevent anyone's pain, friend or stranger. Friendship doesn't create this normative force; it at most modulates our responsibilities regarding it. The normative structure here is: sentience → badness of pain → reasons to prevent it. Friendship enters only at the third stage, if at all.

**Moral status goods**: The reason to respect autonomy—its normative force—comes from personhood itself. This is why we must respect even enemies' autonomy. Again, friendship doesn't generate this authority; personhood does. The normative structure is: personhood → authority of autonomous choice → reasons to respect it.

**Relationship goods**: The reason shared experiences matter—their normative force—exists only because of the friendship. There's no reason to have shared experiences with strangers as such. The normative structure is: friendship → value of shared experience → reasons to pursue it.

The objection says the thesis hasn't shown "friendship cannot provide final reasons to care about" prudential goods even if sentience grounds them. But this misunderstands what showing different value structures means. It's not that friendship provides *no* reasons—it's that the fundamental normative architecture is different. 

When I care about my friend's pain, I'm responding to a reason that exists independently of friendship (the badness of pain for sentient beings), plus perhaps additional friendship-based reasons about priority or responsibility. When I care about shared experiences, I'm responding to a reason that wouldn't exist without friendship. These aren't just different objects of concern with the same value structure—they're different normative structures entirely.

The debate asks: "Does friendship give final or derivative reasons regarding the friend's good?" But for prudential goods, the question is whether friendship modulates pre-existing reasons. For relationship goods, the question is whether friendship creates reasons ex nihilo. These are structurally different questions masquerading as one question.

The objection demands an argument that "different existence conditions entail different value structures." But the thesis observes that these goods already exhibit different value structures (independent normative force vs. friendship-dependent normative force), and that's why they have different existence conditions. The entailment runs the other way.

# VERDICT

The defence fails.

The defence tries to turn the tables by claiming the normative structures are observably different and explain the different grounds, rather than being inferred from them. But this doesn't escape the equivocation—it just relocates it.

The defence claims prudential goods have "independent normative force" while relationship goods have "friendship-dependent normative force." But this is precisely where the equivocation bites. In one sense (existence of reasons), it's true that reasons to prevent pain exist independently of friendship. In another sense (what reasons *I* have), the finality theorist insists that friendship gives me special final reasons regarding *this person's* pain that don't reduce to the general reasons everyone has regarding pain.

The defence says "friendship enters only at the third stage, if at all" for prudential goods, versus creating reasons "ex nihilo" for relationship goods. # BEST DEFENCE

The objection claims "value structure" is too flexible to be testable, but this misreads what the thesis is doing. The thesis isn't proposing an empirical hypothesis that needs falsification criteria—it's diagnosing a conceptual confusion in how a debate is framed. And it does provide clear criteria for what counts as different value structures, even if they weren't explicitly spelled out.

Here are the testable criteria:

**Same value structure**: The reasons friendship gives regarding different goods can be given a unified explanation in terms of a single normative principle or source. For instance: "Friendship gives final reasons to promote whatever contributes to the friend's flourishing" or "Friendship creates derivative reasons that all trace back to impartial duties plus voluntarily-incurred obligations."

**Different value structures**: No such unified explanation is possible because the normative architecture differs. Specifically:
- For prudential goods: reasons exist prior to friendship; friendship at most modulates priority/responsibility
- For moral status goods: reasons exist prior to friendship; friendship doesn't alter the authority structure
- For relationship goods: reasons exist only because of friendship; no prior normative foundation

This IS testable. The finality theorist's unified account—"friendship gives final reasons for all three"—fails the test because it papers over the architectural difference: for prudential/moral goods, there are already reasons present that friendship doesn't create, while for relationship goods, friendship creates the reasons. Saying "friendship gives final reasons" for both is like saying "banks store valuable things" works for both riverbanks (storing sediment) and financial banks (storing money)—true in some abstract sense, but missing that the mechanisms are entirely different.

The thesis predicts: any attempt to give a genuinely unified account will either (a) reduce to verbal similarity that ignores the architectural differences, or (b) fail to accommodate one of the three types of goods. This is falsifiable: show an account that genuinely unifies the normative architecture without ignoring the differences in how reasons relate to friendship.

The objection asks what would count as evidence that goods share a value structure despite different grounds. Answer: if friendship played the same architectural role for both—either creating the reasons for both, or modulating pre-existing reasons for both, or serving as a conduit for more fundamental principles for both. But it doesn't. For relationship goods, friendship is constitutive; for prudential goods, it's modulatory; for moral goods, it's arguably irrelevant to the authority structure.

The charge of unfalsifiability assumes the thesis is making an empirical claim that needs to accommodate all data. But it's making a conceptual claim: that the debate question presupposes a false unity. This is falsifiable by showing the unity is real—that friendship operates the same way normatively across all three domains. The thesis predicts no one can do this without equivocation or reduction.

# VERDICT

The defence fails, though it makes the thesis's position clearer before failing.

The defence provides criteria for different value structures: friendship creates reasons vs. friendship modulates pre-existing reasons vs. friendship is irrelevant. This is helpful. But it reveals the deeper problem: these criteria are themselves contestable in exactly the way the original debate is contestable.

The finality theorist will reject the claim that friendship merely "modulates" pre-existing reasons for prudential goods. They'll insist: "No—friendship creates NEW final reasons regarding this person's welfare that don't reduce to or derive from the general reasons everyone has. Yes, there are general reasons to prevent suffering, but friendship generates an additional, non-derivative reason to care about THIS person's suffering that has its source in the friendship itself."

The defence claims this is "verbal similarity that ignores architectural differences." But that's question-begging. The finality theorist's whole point is that friendship DOES play the same architectural role across all domains—it generates final, non-derivative reasons—even though the objects of those reasons (welfare, autonomy, shared experiences) have different existence conditions.

The thesis needs independent grounds for saying that when the objects of concern have different existence conditions, friendship must be playing different normative roles. But the defence just asserts this: "for prudential goods, there are already reasons present that friendship doesn't create." The finality theorist denies precisely this—they say friendship creates NEW reasons, not just modulates existing ones.

The unfalsifiability charge sticks because the thesis's criteria for "same value structure" are defined in terms that already presuppose the thesis is correct. Any unified account is rejected as "verbal" or "ignoring architectural differences," but the grounds for these rejections are just restatements of the thesis itself. The thesis hasn't provided independent criteria that both sides of the original debate could accept for testing whether a value structure is unified or heterogeneous.

# BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates pluralism about values with a diagnostic claim about dialectical structure. Yes, Anderson, Stocker, and others defend plural values. Yes, the person-regarding/relationship-regarding distinction exists in the literature. But the thesis isn't claiming "friendship involves plural values" (a substantive position). It's claiming "the finality vs. derivative debate presupposes a false univocality that both sides share" (a diagnostic meta-claim).

Consider the dialectical difference:

**Pluralist position**: "Both finality and derivative theories are wrong because they're monistic. The correct view is pluralism—friendship involves multiple irreducibly different values." This is a THIRD POSITION in the debate, competing with the other two.

**This thesis**: "The debate itself is malformed because both sides presuppose there's a unified 'friend's good' whose value structure (final or derivative) is being disputed. But this presupposition is false—the question doesn't have a well-formed answer because it conflates heterogeneous goods." This is a DISSOLUTION of the debate, not a position within it.

The pluralist says: "You're both wrong; I'm right." The thesis says: "You're both asking a confused question—your disagreement rests on a shared false assumption."

Now, the objection might respond: "But pluralists like Kolodny already make this diagnostic point—they say the debate falsely assumes unified value structure." But look at how pluralists actually argue. Kolodny distinguishes relationship reasons from person reasons, then argues relationship reasons have a specific structure (they're non-derivative). This is still TAKING A SIDE on whether certain friendship reasons are final or derivative—he's just being more careful about which reasons he's discussing.

The thesis makes a stronger claim: BOTH the finality question AND the derivative question are malformed when asked about "the friend's good" as a whole, because that phrase doesn't pick out a unified phenomenon. It's not that pluralists are right and monists wrong—it's that the very terms of the debate (final vs. derivative value of the friend's good) presuppose a false unity.

The objection says this is "one existing position within the debate." But if it were, we should be able to identify philosophers who refuse to answer "Does friendship give final or derivative reasons regarding the friend's good?" on the grounds that the question is malformed. Instead, pluralists answer it selectively—"final for relationship goods, derivative for person goods"—which still treats the question as well-formed, just requiring a nuanced answer.

The thesis's distinctive move is not defending pluralism but diagnosing that the debate question itself is confused in a way that both sides (including pluralists who take sides within the debate) have missed. This is the difference between saying "the answer is more complex than you thought" and saying "your question conflates distinct questions that have no unified answer."

# VERDICT

The defence succeeds partially but ultimately cannot save the thesis from a modified version of the objection.

The defence is right that there's a difference between advocating pluralism (a position) and diagnosing a shared false presupposition (a dissolution). And it's true that if pluralists like Kolodny still answer "final for these reasons, derivative for those," they're treating the debate as well-formed rather than dissolved.

However, the defence fails because the thesis itself doesn't consistently maintain the dissolution posture. Look at the thesis's own formulation: it claims these goods "cannot be assimilated to a single value structure." But this is still making a substantive claim about value structure—it's the pluralist claim that there's no unified structure. A true dissolution would say: "The question 'What is the value structure of the friend's good?' is like asking 'What is the function of banks?'—it has no answer because the term is ambiguous."

But the thesis goes further. It claims prudential goods are "grounded in sentience," moral goods in "personhood," and relationship goods in "friendship itself." These are substantive claims about value structure that pluralists make. The thesis then uses these claims to argue against unified accounts—which is exactly what pluralists do.

The defence tries to distinguish "you're both wrong, I'm right" from "your question is confused." But the thesis actually does both. It makes substantive claims about how different goods are grounded (the pluralist position), then uses these claims to argue the debate question is malformed. This is still participating in the debate, just with a meta-level twist.

The modified objection stands: The thesis is not genuinely novel because it combines (1) standard pluralist claims about friendship involving heterogeneous goods with different grounds, and (2) the meta-level claim that this shows the debate is malformed. But (2) only works if (1) is correct—and (1) is already a contested position in the debate. The thesis hasn't dissolved the debate; it's advocated for pluralism with extra dialectical framing.
